Text:
A decrease in blood pressure may indicate one of 3 problems:

{{c1::loss of blood or its fluid components}}

{{c1::loss of vascular tone / insufficient arterial constriction (even without any fluid loss)}}

{{c1::a cardiac pumping problem}}
Back Extra:
Why: pressure needs fluid to push, vessels that squeeze, and a working pump — one failure mode for each.

Cue: compensation (faster heart rate + arterial constriction) can hold the pressure normal at first, whichever cause is at work.

Text: A decreased blood pressure is a {{c1::late::early/late}} sign of shock — the patient is in the {{c1::decompensated::compensated/decompensated}} stage.
Back Extra:
Meaning: decompensated = the critical stage; the compensatory mechanisms can no longer hold the pressure up.

Pitfall: a normal blood pressure never rules out shock — it may be compensation doing the work.

Mechanism: falling circulation → faster heart rate + arterial constriction → skin and extremity flow shunted to the vital organs → BP stays normal until the defenses fail.

Text: A man vomiting blood has kept a rapid pulse with a normal BP; on reassessment his blood pressure begins to fall. The falling BP means he has entered {{c1::decompensated (critical-stage) shock::stage}}.
Back Extra:
Why: the falling pressure marks the moment the compensating heart rate and vasoconstriction can no longer keep up.

Cue: any markedly low BP means vital-organ perfusion is inadequate — pressure and perfusion must be restored to normal.

Text: Some people have chronically high blood pressure caused by {{c1::progressive narrowing of the arteries::vascular change}} that comes with age.
Back Extra: Ex: during an acute episode, a chronically hypertensive patient's pressure can climb even higher than the already-high baseline.

Text: A serious head injury can push the blood pressure {{c1::very high::very high/very low}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: markedly elevated pressure in a trauma patient should raise your suspicion of head injury.

Distinguish: age-related arterial narrowing raises BP chronically — a head injury can spike it acutely.

Text: Abnormally high blood pressure may cause {{c1::a rupture (or other critical damage)::consequence}} in the arterial system.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: low BP starves the vital organs (perfusion failure); very high BP threatens the vessels themselves.

Cue: when pressure climbs, the body's own defenses act to bring it back down.

Text: {{c1::Systolic pressure::BP component}} is {{c2::the arterial pressure surge with each ventricular contraction}}.
Back Extra:
Meaning: systole = the ventricles' contraction phase.

Cue: each surge IS the pulse wave you palpate at the wrist.

Distinguish: diastolic pressure is the residual floor while the heart relaxes.
verified_by: agent; long-cloze warning cleared: two-way definition c2 kept to its 8-word discriminating core (surge + artery + contraction)

Text: {{c1::Diastolic pressure::BP component}} is {{c2::the residual arterial pressure while the heart relaxes}}.
Back Extra:
Meaning: diastole = the relaxing phase of the heart's cycle, when the left ventricle is at rest.

Cue: 'residual' — the floor never drains to zero between beats.

Distinguish: systolic pressure is the surge with each contraction.
verified_by: agent; long-cloze warning cleared: two-way definition c2 kept to its 8-word discriminating core (residual + artery + relaxation)

Text: {{c1::Systolic}} pressure represents the {{c2::maximum::maximum/minimum}} pressure the arteries are subjected to, and {{c1::diastolic}} pressure represents the {{c2::minimum::maximum/minimum}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: blood pressure swings between a ceiling and a floor — the two names label the edges of that swing.

Why: the diastolic minimum never drains away — some pressure is always present in the arteries between beats.
verified_by: agent; editor: stripped 'that is always present in the arteries' from the visible stem — on the c2 card it decoded 'minimum' for a non-knower (always present = the floor), then 'maximum' fell by elimination (#15/#16); the always-present teaching moved to a Back Extra Why line

Text: Blood pressure is measured in {{c1::millimeters of mercury (mm Hg)::unit}}.
Back Extra: Cue: the sphygmomanometer's gauge and your PCR entry use the same unit.

Text:
A patient's systolic pressure is 120 and diastolic pressure is 80. Give the reading two ways:

recorded on the PCR: {{c1::"BP 120/80 mm Hg"::written form}}

reported aloud: {{c1::"120 over 80"::spoken form}}
Back Extra:
Why: blood pressure is reported as a fraction — always systolic over diastolic.

Cue: the spoken form drops the unit; the written form keeps mm Hg.

Text: A normal-size BP cuff is designed to wrap around the arm {{c1::1 to 1.5}} times and take up {{c1::two-thirds::fraction}} of the length from the armpit to the elbow crease.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: a cuff too SMALL reads falsely high; a cuff too LARGE reads falsely low.

Cue: most agencies carry at least three sizes — thigh, adult, and pediatric (plus a large adult).
verified_by: agent; R13 word-check cleared: extractor context has OCR-joined 'twothirds', render p1038 prints 'two-thirds' verbatim

Text: A thigh cuff goes on the arm of patients who are {{c1::obese}} or have {{c1::exceptionally well-developed arm muscles}} — and it takes a thigh BP when {{c1::both arms are injured}}.
Back Extra:
Why: an oversized arm makes the standard cuff effectively too small — and a too-small cuff reads falsely high.

Distinguish: the small pediatric cuff covers children and exceptionally small adults.

Cue: measure a blood pressure in every patient older than 3 years.
verified_by: agent; editor: third use (thigh BP) had been left fully visible — cloze-one-reveal-rest (#5); the CONDITION 'both arms are injured' is now clozed (clozing 'thigh' beside 'thigh cuff' would self-answer, #20/#22); load 3 uncued

Text: In BP auscultation, the inflated cuff compresses the {{c1::brachial}} artery; the turbulence and arterial vibrations it creates are heard as {{c1::Korotkoff::eponym}} sounds. As the cuff is released, the sounds {{c2::appear::appear/disappear}} at the systolic pressure and {{c2::disappear::appear/disappear}} at the diastolic.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: squeezed artery → turbulent flow as blood first returns (sound = systolic); once the artery is fully open the flow runs smooth and silent (silence = diastolic).

Cue: stethoscope over the brachial artery while the cuff bleeds down.
verified_by: agent; R13 word-check cleared: 'appear' paraphrases the context's 'Korotkoff sounds will be heard' (p1039)

Text: Very fit people and patients taking {{c1::beta blockers::drug class}} may have a normal resting heart rate below {{c1::60}} beats/min.
Back Extra: Cue: ask patients their usual pulse and blood pressure — many track heart rate on a smart watch and know their baseline.

Text: A 24-year-old triathlete who feels fine after a minor wrist injury has a resting pulse of 52 beats/min, strong and regular. Most likely explanation: {{c1::a normal variant for a very fit person::normal variant or warning sign}}.
Back Extra:
Why: a very fit person's normal resting rate can sit below 60 beats/min.

Cue: beta blockers produce the same slow-but-normal resting rate — ask about medications and the patient's known baseline.
verified_by: agent; editor: answer re-led with 'a normal variant' so the forced-choice hint's option matches the revealed answer (#13 spelling rule); 52 remains an invented exemplar value consistent with the verified < 60 claim

Text: Measuring BP by palpation uses the cuff plus your fingers on the {{c1::radial::pulse site}} pulse (no stethoscope), and it yields only the {{c1::systolic::systolic/diastolic}} pressure — the other component cannot be determined.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: once you find the pulse, do not move your fingertips until the measurement is done.

Distinguish: auscultation (stethoscope over the brachial artery) yields both pressures.

Cue: either method, the cuff's distal edge sits about 1 in (2.5 cm) above the elbow crease (antecubital space), arm held at heart level.

visual_source.note: PARTIAL marks; both skill drills read on renders

Text:
You took a blood pressure of 120 by palpation. Give it two ways:

recorded on the PCR: {{c1::"120/P"::written form}}

verbalized: {{c1::"120 palpated"::spoken form}}
Back Extra:
Why: the P stands in the diastolic slot because palpation cannot measure one.

Cue: document the time, and note that the pressure was taken by palpation.

visual_source.note: PARTIAL mark; recording conventions read on renders

Text: Taking a BP by palpation, you slowly deflate the cuff and first feel the radial pulse return with the gauge at 96. That 96 is the patient's {{c1::systolic::systolic/diastolic}} pressure.
Back Extra: Cue: the pulse vanishes as the cuff inflates past it and returns as the cuff deflates — the return marks the systolic.

visual_source.note: PARTIAL mark; drill step read on render; the 96 is a fresh exemplar value, not a book number

Text:
Before cuffing an arm for a BP, check for 4 named reasons to use the other arm instead:

{{c1::a dialysis fistula}}

{{c1::central lines / an IV site}}

{{c1::a mastectomy on that side}}

{{c1::an injury to that arm}}
Back Extra:
Cue: the check ends with a catch-all — "or other reason not to use this arm"; when in doubt, switch.

Ex: a dialysis patient with chronic renal failure — ask about a fistula before the cuff goes on.
verified_by: agent; editor: Cue's 'the screen ends' reworded to 'the check ends' (screen scanned as a display); 4 named items re-counted against the p1043 render — matches, catch-all disclosed on the back

visual_source.note: PARTIAL mark; drill step 1 read on render

Text: Inflate the BP cuff until the pulse (or its sounds) disappears, then continue up to {{c1::200}} mm Hg before starting the slow release.
Back Extra:
Why: overshooting guarantees the cuff starts above the systolic point, so the first returning tap or pulse is the true systolic.

Cue: the same 200 mm Hg target applies by auscultation and by palpation.

visual_source.note: 200 mm Hg verified in both drills on renders

Text: As a BP cuff deflates, the gauge needle often bounces in time with the pulsation — those needle movements {{c1::are not::are/are not}} the patient's blood pressure.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: with a very low BP, the sounds can continue all the way down — record the diastolic as "0" (heard until the gauge read 0).

Cue: pressures come from the sounds (or the returning pulse), never from needle motion.

Text: What is the normal systolic blood pressure range for an adult? {{c1::90 to 120::range}} mm Hg
Back Extra:
Meaning: below the normal range = hypotension; above it = hypertension.

Cue: the most important BP information is often the trend over time, not any single value.

Text: What is the normal systolic blood pressure range for an adolescent (15 years)? {{c1::110 to 131::range}} mm Hg
Back Extra: Cue: blood pressure levels vary with age and sex — normal ranges are guidelines, not absolutes.

Text: What is the normal systolic blood pressure range for a child (7 years)? {{c1::97 to 115::range}} mm Hg
Back Extra: Cue: you see children less often — carrying a chart of pediatric normal ranges is expected practice.

Text: What is the normal systolic blood pressure range for a child (2 years)? {{c1::86 to 106::range}} mm Hg
Back Extra: Cue: readings vary with the patient and how they react to the environment around them.
verified_by: agent; editor: trimmed the ungrounded 'a frightened toddler runs high' extrapolation (#3 grounding) — kept the p1049-grounded reaction-to-environment claim

Text: What is the normal systolic blood pressure range for an infant (1–12 months)? {{c1::72 to 104::range}} mm Hg
Back Extra: Distinguish: the neonate band covers only the first 96 hours; infant = 1 to 12 months.

Text: What is the normal systolic blood pressure range for a neonate (96 hours)? {{c1::67 to 84::range}} mm Hg
Back Extra: Distinguish: the neonate band covers the first 96 hours of life; from 1 month on, the infant band applies.
